title: Texas halts new data centers as governor calls for audits
author: Modelverse Editorial
excerpt: Tech companies and developers have been scouring the U.S. for places to build data centers, and they’ve been drawn to Texas’ loose regulations and seemingly abundant power supply. ...
body:
## Texas Halts New Data Center Projects Amid Grid Strain Concerns

Texas Governor Greg Abbott has introduced a significant policy shift, mandating comprehensive audits for all new data center developments. This move comes as the state, a major hub for data infrastructure, grapples with an unprecedented surge in electricity demand. Historically attractive for its relaxed regulations and ample power, Texas now faces potential grid overwhelm, with data center interconnection requests more than doubling in six months to 474 gigawatts. This represents a critical pivot for a state that has been a magnet for tech companies seeking to expand their computing infrastructure.

Under the new directive, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) will scrutinize proposed projects. This includes evaluating projected electricity and water consumption, noise and light pollution controls, tax incentive use, and ownership structures. The aim is to prevent a scenario where the sheer volume of proposed data centers—representing over five times ERCOT's current peak demand—could destabilize the state's power supply and drive up energy costs, a trend already observed with the proliferation of such facilities.

For AI and tech developers and researchers, this signals a critical shift in the data center landscape. Texas, once a go-to location for its operational advantages, now presents a more complex regulatory environment. This increased oversight means longer planning cycles, potentially higher compliance expenses, and a re-evaluation of site selection strategies. The decision underscores a growing national conversation about the sustainability and infrastructure demands of rapidly expanding AI and high-performance computing, potentially prompting other regions to consider similar measures to manage the immense energy footprint of modern tech infrastructure.
